newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Ampros to sell city centre properties.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Ampros to sell city centre properties.

text.p: South African holding firm Anglo American Property Services Ltd (Ampros) said on Tuesday it plans to sell 300 million rands worth of city centre properties as part of a restructuring of three of its listed units.
The firms involved in the rejig are Apex Property Fund , Compass Property Holdings and Anglo American Properties Ltd. A fourth listed unit, Main Street Property, will continue with its present focus.

"The objective of the disposals is to accelerate Apex's strategy to become a decentralised office fund, to bring greater focus to Compass and to restructure Amaprop's portfolio to exclude direct property investments," Ampros managing director Gerald Leissner said in a statement.
Each of the three firms owns about 100 million rands worth of property in the central business districts (CBDs) of Johannesburg, Pretoria, Durban and Cape Town.

The decision to sell comes after the CBD properties suffered write-downs of about 340 million rand over the last two years due to increasing vacancies and lower rentals. The average vacancy rate is now about 25 percent in these properties.
South Africa's city centres have suffered heavily at the hands of the country's notorious crime wave and many businesses have fled to business parks built in more suburban locations.
In April Sanlam Properties, South Africa's largest investor, said it would freeze investment plans in the countries crime-ridden CBDs until action was taken to lure business back.
Leissner said Compass would ultimately sell its entire portfolio -- of which CBD buildings were about a third -- and plough the cash back into other properties.
Ampaprop would change its focus from direct property ownership to investment in listed and unlisted property vehicles.

"Amaprop will effectively be stripped of all its direct property investments in a bid to realise the underlying value of this portfolio, as the share has been trading at a substantial discount to net asset value," Leissner said.
The cash raised from the sale of Apex's CBD assets will be reinvested in properties away from city centres on the basis that any acquisitions do not materially dilute earnings.
"Apex may have to sit on cash until it can buy at reasonable yields, in order not to dilute earnings," Leissner said.
